title: Why Do We Still Have Final Exams?
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Potkalitsky questions the high school final exam, arguing it clashes with authentic, continuous assessment and with student and teacher wellbeing. He gives five grounds: a single snapshot cannot capture learning, exam periods create harmful stress, endemic illness makes fixed schedules unfair, grading loads erode teachers' breaks, and high-stakes exams compound socioeconomic disparities. Throughout he adds a conditional fallback, saying that if schools keep finals they should reformulate them as one assessment among many, with choice, support and flexible timing. His closing proposal is to hold exams a week or two before term ends so make-ups and grading finish in time and the last week becomes a reflective, metacognitive review. The argument leans on cited news items more than original evidence, but its practical redesign of the exam calendar is clear.
points: Finals offer only a snapshot, so schools should treat them as one assessment among many and give students choice and multiple chances to show competence.
Exam stress is an avoidable cost; a final should assess skills rather than test endurance under pressure.
Fixed, unforgiving exam schedules are poorly suited to winters with endemic illness and should be made adaptable.
Marking finals over break eats into teachers' rest, so grading should be scheduled to finish on campus before the holiday.
Moving finals earlier frees the last week for make-up exams, review and student reflection on the course itself.
quotes: If schools insist on having final exams, they need to reformulate them so that they are only one assessment among many. Ideally, they should involve choice so that they have multiple opportunities to demonstrate skill and content competency.

The goal of a final is to assess skills. The objective should not be to replicate a high-pressure environment reminiscent of our own school days, where the bulk of the assessment hinged on the student's capacity to withstand stress.
These exams do not account for this cyclical rise in illnesses, especially during winter months, which conflicts with the principles of fair and flexible assessment.

Grading essays or exams for 10-20 hours over a break does not constitute an actual break from school activities. If schools continue to insist on final exams, they should develop grading schedules that allow for teachers to complete final records while on campus.

Some students have more resources to lean into during final exam schedules. Some students can secure quiet study spaces by getting rides to and from school. Some students come from families who have generations of experiences tackling difficult summative exam experiences. But many do not.

If schools are determined to retain final exams, it would be advisable to schedule them 1 or 2 weeks before the semester's end. In this way, students will have the opportunity to make-up missed exams and revise completed for the final if a teacher is open to alternative assessment strategies.

In addition, a final week could blossom into a truly reflective time and space where we empower students to do the big metacognitive work of surveying group covered, evaluating pathways taken, and mapping out trajectories for future engagements.
